newsitem.title: UK: BA does not rule out delay in American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA does not rule out delay in American deal.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Wednesday there could be a delay in starting its proposed alliance with American Airlines next April as planned, if it cannot win government approvals in time.
Chief executive Robert Ayling said in reply to questioning at a company news conference that the important thing was to get the necessary approvals sooner or later.
"The important thing is to get this deal done and we are doing everything we can this week and next week to make sure that it is done and that's the important thing, not the start date."
"If we can achieve it by the first of April so much the better but if we can't then we would rather wait," he said.
American said earlier this month that a delay was likely because Britain and the U.S. have yet to agree the "open skies" aviation trade pact needed for the deal to be approved.
In a related move the British government was still waiting for advice from its Office of Fair Trading (OFT) as to whether the deal should be blocked on competition grounds.
Industry sources said on Tuesday that there was some speculation the OFT would make its report to trade minister Ian Lang on Friday.

Ayling said in a speech on the airline's new business plan to 300 BA managers earlier on Wednesday that the proposed alliance with American was a key part of its strategy to "build a global network with a presence in all major markets."
"I am determined our agreement with them should be approved, though not at any price," he said.
BA and American's plans have attracted fierce criticism from rival airlines as well as consumer groups, who say the alliance will dominate the London trans-Atlantic market.

Under the alliance, BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
They would also combine their frequent flyer programmes and share flight booking codes to promote their connecting flights on computer reservation systems.
BA and American argue that their deal will lead to greater competition on transatlantic routes because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree "open skies".
But talks between government negotiators broke down last month.

Industry sources say the main sticking points have been that American's U.S. rivals want their government to secure some of BA's 38 percent share of runway slots at London's Heathrow airport and also to be given "fifth freedom" rights to fly from Britain to third countries.

In return BA says it should not have to give up slots. But also the sources say British government negotiators have been asking for rights for British airlines to fly domestic routes within the United States.
This has been a key request made by BA's arch rival Virgin Atlantic Airways, they said.
